sections.title: Anatomi Sistem Vestibularis

content.text: The vestibular system has peripheral and central components. Peripheral structures include the vestibular apparatus and vestibular nerve (cranial nerve VIII). Central structures include the brainstem (vestibular nuclei), thalamus, cerebral cortex, and cerebellum. Central vertigo specifically localizes to lesions along the central vestibular pathway from the nucleus vestibularis in the brainstem through the thalamus to the cerebral cortex.
Perifer: Aparatus vestibularis, Nervus Vestibularis
Sentral: Batang Otak, Talamus, Korteks, Cerebellum

sections.title: Etiologi dan Manifestasi Klinis Vertigo Sentral

content.text: Central vertigo is not an independent disease but a symptom of underlying pathology affecting the central vestibular system. The etiology determines the clinical presentation and guides management.

ACUTE ONSET ETIOLOGIES: Vascular causes (stroke, TIA) and post-traumatic diffuse axonal injury are the most common acute presentations, requiring immediate neuroimaging and stroke protocol evaluation.

SUBACUTE/CHRONIC/EPISODIC ETIOLOGIES: Multiple sclerosis presents with spinning dizziness, decreased visual acuity with painful eye movements, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, blurred vision, diplopia, balance disturbance, and CN VIII involvement. Treatment involves corticosteroids and interferon for relapsing-remitting disease. CPA tumors (most commonly vestibular schwannoma) present with unilateral hearing loss, vestibular symptoms, trigeminal nerve dysfunction (facial numbness, pain), headache, vision decline, ataxia, and hemiparesis. Primary treatment is surgical, with options including observation, radiotherapy/stereotactic radiosurgery, and microsurgery. Prognosis depends on tumor size and severity of neurological deficits at diagnosis. Epilepsy vestibular type arises from focal lesions in the superior temporal gyrus or parietal association cortex receiving ipsilateral thalamic vestibular projections. Symptoms include episodic floating/rotating sensations, either as seizure aura or psychomotor seizure manifestation. Management focuses on seizure control with antiepileptic drugs. Traumatic central vertigo is a common sequela of head and neck trauma including diffuse axonal injury, presenting as central vestibular syndrome from brainstem dysfunction. Management includes pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches, with surgical intervention when indicated.
Onset classification helps narrow differential: acute = vascular/trauma; subacute-chronic = inflammatory, neoplastic, or degenerative

sections.title: Pendekatan Diagnosis Etiologi

content.text: The diagnostic workup for central vertigo should systematically evaluate for the underlying cause. Key questions include: Is central vertigo clinically confirmed? Has supportive diagnostic testing been performed? Are there differential diagnoses to consider? Once the diagnosis is established, treatment targets the specific etiology: acute stroke management, head trauma protocols, intracranial pressure reduction for infection or tumor, and other cause-specific interventions.

sections.title: Tatalaksana Vertigo Sentral

content.text: Symptomatic treatment aims to reduce the two main symptom clusters: the vertigo sensation (spinning, floating) and autonomic symptoms (nausea, vomiting). Vestibular suppressants are divided into three pharmacological groups.
Antikolinergik: scopolamine
Antihistamin: dimenhydrinate, cinnarizine
Benzodiazepine: diazepam, lorazepam
Antiemetik: metoclopramide, ondansetron
Rehidrasi: infus, NGT jika diperlukan
Three groups of vestibular suppressants: anticholinergics, antihistamines, benzodiazepines

sections.title: Tatalaksana Lanjutan dan Indikasi Rujuk

content.text: Central vestibular vertigo requires definitive diagnosis of the underlying etiology and appropriate definitive treatment. Referral is indicated when: (1) Facilities for diagnostic confirmation and etiology-specific management are needed (e.g., suspected stroke requiring non-contrast CT head and neurology specialist consultation); (2) No improvement is seen after pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment.
Penegakan diagnosis untuk etiologi vertigo diperlukan
Tatalaksana definitif untuk etiologi diperlukan
Indikasi rujuk: butuh fasilitas diagnosis dan tatalaksana etiologi (contoh: curiga stroke, butuh CT-scan kepala nonkontras dan SpN)
Tidak terdapat perbaikan setelah terapi farmakologik maupun non-farmakologik

sections.title: Rehabilitasi

content.text: Rehabilitation is performed after the underlying disease has been managed and no longer poses acute health concerns requiring immediate therapy. The goals of rehabilitation are: to improve gaze stability, enhance postural body stability, prevent recurrent vertigo, and improve the patient's ability to perform daily activities independently. Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT) is a highly effective modality for improving functional deficits and subjective complaints resulting from unilateral or bilateral vestibular hypofunction and central balance disorders in both adults and children.

diagnostic_logic.title: Confirm central vs peripheral vertigo
diagnostic_logic.explanation: Central vertigo localizes to brainstem, thalamus, cortex, or cerebellum; peripheral involves vestibular apparatus or vestibular nerve

diagnostic_logic.title: Determine onset pattern
diagnostic_logic.explanation: Acute onset suggests vascular or traumatic cause; subacute/chronic/episodic suggests inflammatory, neoplastic, or migrainous etiology

diagnostic_logic.title: Apply neuroimaging and appropriate workup
diagnostic_logic.explanation: CT head for acute presentations, MRI for detailed CNS evaluation, additional testing as indicated by suspected etiology

diagnostic_logic.title: Initiate cause-specific treatment
diagnostic_logic.explanation: Stroke protocol for vascular causes, corticosteroids for MS, surgery for CPA tumors, antiepileptics for seizure-related vertigo

differential_notes.how_to_separate: Subacute onset with internuclear ophthalmoplegia, visual changes, and CN VIII involvement; requires MRI and clinical observation over time
Progressive unilateral hearing loss with trigeminal signs, ataxia; MRI with contrast is diagnostic
Acute onset with vascular risk factors; neuroimaging confirms
History of head/neck trauma, often diffuse axonal injury pattern
Brief episodic vertigo as aura or psychomotor seizure component; EEG and temporal lobe imaging

treatment_notes.content: Treat underlying etiology: stroke management, trauma protocols, ICP reduction for infection/tumor, corticosteroids and interferon for MS relapses
Vestibular suppressants (anticholinergics, antihistamines, benzodiazepines), antiemetics (metoclopramide, ondansetron), rehydration
